turn1.explanation: The unit fires on clause- and sentence-boundary punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) in documents whose earlier context contains ship or boat vocabulary such as ship, boat, vessel, anchor, crew or sailing. It acts like a nautical-context flag that is read out at punctuation, not on the nautical words themselves.
turn1.evidence: Nearly every example mentions ships or boats (SeaArk boats 4.19, powerships 4.19, cruise-ship casino 4.16, listed ships, flying-boats, V.Ships, Stargate ship, cargo ship, the sunken rig). Weaker documents have only indirect cues: 'Anchor' electronics (~3.4), 'anchor' text in the SEO post (~3.1), blood 'vessels' in the radiology report (~2), 'Sailing the Antarsa' (~1.7). In all of them the nouns themselves get near-zero activation and only the following punctuation lights up.
turn1.missing_data: The most useful tests are a ship-heavy document checked for punctuation activation versus the same punctuation in a matched document with no nautical words. It would also help to see whether other homographs (vessel, anchor, crew) trigger it reliably and whether this list-style punctuation fires without any ship context, as in the news-broadcast example.
